extracted.intended_audience: readers of Popular Science Monthly — educated public, scientists, and higher-education faculty/administrators
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing the adequacy and balance of college curricula (science vs. classics), including course offerings, laboratory resources, and the teaching of hygiene/physiology; also addresses standards for scientific study of society and methods for experimental observation in natural history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Due combination of literature, science, and philosophy
rubrics_metrics.description: I believe that, in our higher educational institutions, there should be a due combination of literature (including languages), of science, and philosophy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose is 'developing the man and the full man.' Do not regard a youth as fully trained who knows merely Latin and Greek, nor one who knows only his own bodily frame and malarial disease. Curricula should balance humanistic and scientific studies rather than subordinating one to the other.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching of hygiene, anatomy, and physiology
rubrics_metrics.description: "All students of the college have a full course of instruction in the outlines of human anatomy and physiology, with so much of hygiene as there is time for"; and "let the knowledge that conduces to self-preservation be taught first and thoroughly."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hygiene and physiology should be taught adequately to yield beneficent results (preventable catastrophes). If textbooks or teachers are inadequate or incompetent, replace them to ensure effective instruction in knowledge essential to self-preservation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provision of adequate scientific instruction resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of adequacy includes numbers of science courses and teachers (e.g., 44 science courses vs. 12 classical courses; growth from 5 to 24 science teachers), and laboratory capacity (physical, botanical, physiological, chemical laboratories with personal experiment tables).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Universities should provide ample laboratory appliances and personal experimentation stations, support original investigators, and expand facilities when demand outstrips supply (e.g., enlarge buildings to add more tables). Quantity of courses and instructional staff and up-to-date appliances are metrics of institutional commitment to science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom of student choice in studies
rubrics_metrics.description: The University has long held up as its ideal: 'All learning and that of the best'; and entire freedom of choice on the part of students as to what they would pursue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions should not preclude particular studies by prescriptive fiat; students should be free to choose scientific or classical pathways without institutional coercion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority for knowledge that conduces to self-preservation
rubrics_metrics.description: We only say, let the knowledge that conduces to self-preservation be taught first and thoroughly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When curricular time is limited, prioritize instruction (e.g., hygiene, sanitation) that directly prevents public-health failures; if existing teaching is superficial due to 'old crowded classical curriculum,' reform ordering and quality of instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific study of society requires systematic, rigorous method
rubrics_metrics.description: By the science of society is meant such a systematic exposition of the facts and relations of social phenomena as shall bring out the natural laws of social change and transformation. The doctrine of evolution compels the study of society from a scientific point of view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political/social scholarship should trace and formulate determinable laws of political change, apply rigorous scientific method, overcome prejudices and lax thinking, and be precise about the scope of works when critiquing (examine the works where the theory is actually expounded rather than side discussions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of culture/ethnical periods by development of arts
rubrics_metrics.description: These grand periods... were set forth as the savage, the barbaric, and the civilized. These were defined in terms relating to the evolution of arts. Savagery and barbarism were divided into three periods each, giving the lower, middle, and upper status of savagery, and the lower, middle, and upper status of barbarism; these subdivisions also being established on the development of specified arts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing cultures historically, use specified arts and technological evolution as the basis for periodization and subdivision; document the development of arts as evidence for placing societies in stages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization of government forms and their evolutionary order
rubrics_metrics.description: Two grand plans of government are also set forth — tribal and national; tribal government being personal, i.e., taking into account persons only, and national government being territorial and based on property. He discussed different forms of government in the order of their evolution, beginning with organization upon the basis of sex, then kinship-based tribal governments, and the evolution of gentile society into property society and national government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate political institutions by tracing their evolution from sex-based to kinship-based (gentes, phratries, tribes, confederacies) to property-based national governments; use wide comparative evidence to infer universality of stages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analysis of family evolution via successive forms
rubrics_metrics.description: He treats of the evolution of the family — discovers five successive forms, and sets forth the processes by which the first or consanguineal family ... was developed into the last or monogamian, which is founded upon marriage by single pairs with exclusive cohabitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study family institutions by identifying successive structural forms and the social processes transforming one form to the next; present sequences (e.g., tabular form with appended explanations) to make institutional evolution clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological standards for animal navigation/experimental observation
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples: bee hunter marks direction of released bees and finds hive at intersection of lines; frog experiment — mark individuals (cut toes), displace them (carry in bag, whirl to confuse orientation), release at a distant point, and later recapture or identify return to origin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design experiments to control for confounds (e.g., prevent visual tracking of handler by transporting and spinning the specimen), uniquely mark individuals for identification, record directions and repeated observations, and consider alternative explanations (e.g., following tracks vs innate sense of direction). Document chains of custody and timing of observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholarly precision in critiquing large systematic works
rubrics_metrics.description: It is hardly fair to an author to mix up his works in this careless way... President Porter's critical essay is entitled 'Spencer's Theory of Sociology,' and he says, 'The only practicable method of discovering the author's theory is to subject the volume to a minute criticism.' We think the still more 'practicable' method would be an examination of the works in which the theory is professedly expounded rather than in a volume which disavows all attempt to formulate the principles of the science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating an author's theory, critique the works where the theory is actually developed; avoid judging an author's systematic theory by incidental or side-discussion volumes. Be particular about scope and avoid careless conflation of separate works.
